t: Count Islands With Total Value Divisible by K
o: This is a classic connected-components problem with a twist: instead of counting islands, we count only those whose cell values sum to a multiple of $k$. An island is a maximal set of positive cells (value > 0) connected 4-directionally; zeros are water and break connectivity. In Example 1, the four positive clusters have sums like 8 (2+5+1), 13 (5+1+7... per cluster), etc., and exactly two of them sum to multiples of 5. In Example 2, six single-cell islands each hold value 3, so all 6 qualify. With up to $10^5$ cells, any linear-time flood-fill (DFS/BFS) or union-find pass works; recursion depth up to $10^5$ means recursive DFS risks stack overflow in some languages, so iterative traversal or increased limits are safer.
k: Only cells with value > 0 are land; zeros act as water separators.
Each island is an independent connected component — find it once, sum its cells, check sum % k == 0.
With m*n up to 10^5, prefer iterative BFS/DFS to avoid deep recursion stacks.

a.i: Scan the grid; whenever we hit an unvisited positive cell, that's a new island. Flood-fill its entire component using an explicit stack/queue, accumulating the sum of cell values along the way. After filling, increment the answer if the accumulated sum is divisible by $k$. Each cell is visited exactly once, giving linear time.
s: Initialize visited matrix (or modify grid in place) and answer = 0.
For each cell (i, j): if grid[i][j] > 0 and not visited, start a flood fill from it.
During the fill, pop cells from a stack, add their values to a running sum, mark visited, and push unvisited positive 4-directional neighbors.
When the component is exhausted, if sum % k == 0, increment answer.
a.t: O(m * n) — every cell is pushed and popped at most once during all flood fills.
a.sp: O(m * n) — for the visited matrix and worst-case stack size.

a.i: Treat each positive cell as a node and union adjacent positive cells. Maintain a running sum per root so merging components keeps totals correct. Finally, count distinct roots whose stored sum is divisible by $k$. This generalizes naturally to dynamic connectivity variants where edges arrive over time.
s: Map each positive cell to an index; initialize parent arrays and sum[i] = grid value at that cell.
For each pair of adjacent positive cells, union their sets.
Union by size/rank with path compression; when merging roots a and b, add sum[a] into sum[b].
After processing all cells, count indices i that are roots (find(i) == i) with sum[i] % k == 0.
a.t: O(m * n * α(m * n)) — near-linear due to inverse Ackermann from path compression and union by size.
a.sp: O(m * n) — for parent, size, and sum arrays.

w: In an interview, lead with the iterative BFS/DFS flood fill — it's the expected optimal answer, simple to code correctly, and avoids recursion-depth issues on grids up to 10^5 cells. Mention union-find as an alternative if the interviewer asks about dynamic edge insertion or streaming updates. Common pitfalls: (1) treating zero cells as land — they must be excluded since islands consist only of positive integers; (2) using recursive DFS in Python/Java and hitting stack overflow on large snake-like islands; (3) integer overflow when summing up to 10^5 cells of value 10^6 (max ~10^11), which requires 64-bit sums in C++/Java; (4) forgetting to mark cells visited when pushing them onto the stack, causing duplicates. Edge cases: all-zero grid returns 0, k larger than any island sum still counts islands whose sum equals 0? No — sums are positive since cells are positive, so divisibility checks behave normally. Likely follow-ups: count islands divisible by k after adding/removing land cells (union-find with rollback or offline processing), or handle 8-directional connectivity.
